The Raavad's objection was based on a corrupt reading caused by a copyist's error, which is the reading reproduced by the Tur, as the Kesef Mishneh and Beit Yosef explain. The verified reading cited by the Maggid Mishneh is the reading in our books. It is then clear that where there was despair by the owner together with a change of possession, the purchaser certainly acquires the object. Nevertheless, if he purchased from a notorious thief, although he acquires the item and need not return the object itself, he must return its value. If he purchased from a thief who was not notorious, then because of the market regulation he need not even return the money. The Bach proves from several sources that the purchaser returns the money, but deducts from the value of the object that he gives the owner the amount that he himself paid the thief, because of the market regulation. In Perishah he writes that Maharam's principle, that the excess is returned, resolves several difficulties in the Tur and Rambam. The Kesef Mishneh discusses at length the rejection of the version quoted by the Tur, and this is not the place to elaborate.

Whether with his body, etc. Meaning the injured party's body, as explained below, and likewise the injured party's property. This is as stated there concerning one who brought an object in and one who entered, showing that the rules are equal. The same applies where the householder caused the damage. Only where one filled another's courtyard did they say that the owner may break his way out. See Tosafot there.

And specifically where he damaged him, etc.; if both had permission, etc. This entire passage is Tur's wording, but it is difficult, because it combines Rashi's approach with Rambam's. Lechem Mishneh already raised this issue. According to Rambam, where the damager has permission, where both have permission, or where neither has permission, the laws are equal: intentional damage is liable, and unintentional damage is exempt. When the damage occurs in the injured party's domain, however, the damager is liable even unintentionally. This is Rambam's explanation of the Gemara. Rashi's approach differs: where both have permission or neither has permission, one who actively damages is liable even without intent, but one who is injured automatically is exempt. In the injured party's domain the entrant is always liable, while in the damager's domain he is always exempt unless he knew of the entrant, in which case it is as though both had permission. Thus Rambam and Shulchan Aruch in seif 4 refer specifically to the injured party's domain. In the public domain, Rambam equates it with the damager's domain, requiring intent, whereas Rashi imposes liability for active damage even without intent. This also explains the different readings of the Gemara. See 50 and 81.

And some say, etc. Ramah follows Rashi's approach, but adds that if the householder knew of the entrant, both are treated as having equal permission even regarding the entrant, so if the householder was injured through him he is exempt. Rav Pappa's distinction applies to both clauses, though its principal novelty concerns the latter. The statement that where he knew they are both 'with permission' should read 'both without permission.' This is clear from the Mishna: where each proceeds normally, both have permission; if one stops, one has permission and the other does not; if one warns the other, both are without permission. See 80 and 81.

We rule otherwise, following Rafram, who compelled Rav Ashi to pay. The Rambam likewise rules this way in law 8, although he does not state it explicitly because he had a somewhat different textual reading and explanation of Rava's words, as the Maggid Mishneh writes.

heh) The Rosh explains in his rulings in the name of Rabbeinu Yitzchak that liability applies where he did not perform an act upon the damaged object itself, and writes that this is the reasonable distinction. Tosafot likewise write this in the name of Rabbeinu Yitzchak at the end of Bava Batra 22b. He further writes another distinction, that dina d'garmi applies where the damage follows immediately from the act.

vav) I searched and did not find that Tosafot or the Rosh explicitly ruled like Rabba to exempt one who pushes another's coin into the sea or defaces it. According to the two distinctions Tosafot and the Rosh give in chapter Lo Yachpor, it appears that they would impose liability in both cases, because the person acts directly upon the damaged object and the loss follows immediately from the act.

zayin) See there at the end of 26b, where Tosafot challenge Rabbeinu Yitzchak's distinctions from the case of one who declared a tamei item tahor and the owner then mixed it with his produce: why is he liable, since he did not damage the other's property directly, and the damage did not occur at the moment of his ruling? Tosafot therefore conclude that dina d'garmi is a penalty imposed for common and frequent forms of damage, as indicated by the Yerushalmi. The Rosh, however, writes that what the owner subsequently does on the basis of his ruling is treated as though the first person performed the act. The Sema ruled regarding a gentile who concluded a commercial agreement with one Jew for a certain amount of distilled liquor at a set price in the customary merchant fashion of striking hands, and then went to another Jew intending to purchase from him if he offered a lower price. When the first Jew realized this, he asked the second not to sell because the deal had already been concluded, but the second nevertheless sold to the gentile, who then bought from him instead of the first. The Sema rules that the second Jew is not penalized, absent deceptive conduct as assessed by the judges, because he did not pursue the customer and the gentile came to him on his own. Even though the first Jew asked him not to transact, the first cannot require the second to incur a loss for his benefit. The second also has the argument that perhaps the gentile would still purchase the agreed amount from the first. The Sema discusses the matter further.

he_segments: י) ל' הרמב"ם שם בפ"ג ד"י וכתב הכ"מ מימרא דאילפא ורבי אושעיא שם דף כ' ע"א וכדמפרש רבא בקופצת וכמ"ש הנ"י וז"ל פי' קופצת היינו שזקפה רגליה ועמדה על הבהמה ואכלה זקופה אבל אם עמדה מעט כדי לפשוט צוארה פטורה משום דבהמתו לאו כרשות הניזק גמור הוא
פי' וחשיב כר"ה טור

כ) טור וכן כתב הרשב"א וקופצ' דקאמר (רבא שם אמימר' דרבי אושעיא) שקפצה על האדם שהקופה מופשלת לאחוריו וכן ע"ג אנטבא שבר"ה כיון דאורחה למיכל שעורים או כרשינין שבקופה אף היא דרכה לקפוץ שם וטעם חיובן של אלו מפני שהם כחצר הניזק ואע"פ שהם עומדים בר"ה מפני שיש להם רשות לעבור שם עם משאן
en_segments: yud) The language of the Rambam, chapter 3, law 10. The Kesef Mishneh cites Ilfa and Rabbi Oshaya's statements on 20a, as Rava explains them regarding jumping. The Nimukei Yosef explains that 'jumping' means that the animal raised its legs and stood upon the other animal, eating while upright. But if it merely stood slightly so as to stretch out its neck, it is exempt, because the other person's animal is not fully equivalent to the injured party's domain. The Tur explains that otherwise it is treated as the public domain.

kaf) The Tur and Rashba write that Rava's reference to jumping means that the animal jumped upon a person carrying a basket behind him, or onto a platform in the public domain. Since it is normal for the animal to eat barley or vetch from the basket, it is also normal for it to jump there. The reason for liability in these cases is that they are treated like the injured party's courtyard, even though located in the public domain, because those persons have permission to pass there with their loads.

ב) מבריי' האשה שנכנסה לטחון וכו' שם ע"ב וכן כ' הרשב"א אם הוחלקה והוזקה בהמתו של בעל הבית וה"ה אם אכלתן בהמתו של ב"ה נמי פטור
ונלפע"ד שהגה זו קאי אחלוקה שניה מ"ש ואם קיבל עליו וכו' ומקומה בסוף הסעיף ומחלוקתה מבואר בס"ס שנ"ח

ג) כרבי שם במשנה וכשמואל דפכק כוותיה בגמ' שם דף מ"מ ע"ב וכתב ה"ה ואף רבי לא אמרה דבעי קבלה בפי' אלא להתחייב בעל הבית בנזקי בעל הפירות אבל להפטר בעל הפירות מנזקי בעל החצר כיון שהרשהו להכנס פטור ונכון הוא וכן דעת התו' וגם הרא"ה הודה לו בהשגות
en_segments: a) The language of the Rambam, chapter 3 of Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon, law 14, from the Mishnah in the fifth chapter of Bava Kamma 47a.

bet) From the baraita concerning a woman who entered to grind there on 47b. The Rashba likewise writes that if she slipped and the homeowner's animal was injured, she is exempt, and likewise if the homeowner's animal ate the produce she is exempt. In my humble opinion, this gloss refers to the second clause, 'if he accepted responsibility,' and belongs at the end of the seif. Its dispute is explained at the end of siman 358.

gimel) Following Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi in the Mishnah and Shmuel, who rules accordingly on 48b. The Maggid Mishneh writes that even Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi required explicit acceptance only in order to make the homeowner liable for damage to the entrant's produce. But to exempt the owner of the produce from damage caused to the homeowner's property, once he had permission to enter he is exempt. This is correct, and Tosafot agree; even the Raah conceded this in his glosses.

he_segments: א) ל' הרמב"ם בפ"ג מהנ"מ די"א משנה רפ"ו דב"ק דף נ"ה ע"א
ב) כדמפרש רב כהנא שם דף נ"ח ע"א

פרש"י דהיה לו לשמרה שלא תרד
ז) פסק כרב כהנא וכתב ה"ה שפסק בפסק ההלכות וכתב הב"י דפשטא דגמ' כוותיהו

ח) פסקו כרבא דמפרש מתניתין נפלה לגינה וכו' בשדחפוה חברותיה ופי' ☜פטור לשלם מה שהזוקה אבל חייב לשלם מה שנהנית פשוט ומבואר שם בגמ' וכ"כ הרא"ש בשם התוספת ולא דמי לעובדא דאדא סבולאה בפ"ז דב"מ דף צ"ג ע"ג ואיתא לעיל סימן ש"ג סי"א דחייבוה לשלם לאו משום פשיעה חייביה אלא משום שהיה ש"ש וזה חשוב כגניבה ואבידה כדמשמע התם וכשם שהבעלים פטורים אם דחפה חבירתה כך שומר שכר שלו פטור דהא תנן מסר לש"ח וכו' כלן נכנסו תחת הבעלים בפ"ד דב"ק סוף דף מ"ד ע"ב
en_segments: a) The language of the Rambam, chapter 3 of Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon, law 11, from the Mishnah at the beginning of the sixth chapter of Bava Kamma 55a.
bet) As Rav Kahana explains on 58a.
gimel) As the Gemara explains that Rav stated one case and certainly the more obvious one.
dalet) As Rabbi Yochanan says there.
heh) Ibid., in the Mishnah.

vav) Rabbi Yirmiyah's question on 58a. According to the view that initial negligence followed by an unavoidable accident is exempt, the question arises, but according to the view that such a person is liable it is obvious that he is liable, and we follow that latter view. Rashi explains that he should have guarded the animal so that it would not descend.
zayin) The ruling follows Rav Kahana. The Maggid Mishneh writes that the Rif rules so, and the Beit Yosef writes that the plain Gemara supports them.

chet) They rule like Rava, who explains the Mishnah's case of an animal falling into a garden as one where other animals pushed it. The meaning is that the owner is exempt from paying for the damage the animal caused, but must pay for the benefit it received. This is straightforward in the Gemara. The Rosh writes likewise in the name of Tosafot. This is unlike the incident of Ada Sabolaah in Bava Metzia 93b, cited above in siman 303, seif 11, where liability was imposed not because of negligence but because he was a paid guardian, and such a loss is treated like theft or loss. Just as the owner is exempt when another animal pushed it, so too his paid guardian is exempt, for the Mishnah in the fourth chapter of Bava Kamma at the end of 44b teaches that when the owner transferred the animal to a guardian, all guardians enter in place of the owner.

ג) נלע"ד שלמדו מהא דאמר רבא שם את"ל המשסה כלבו של חבירו בחבירו חייב וכו' משמע ליה דנפשטא הבעיא אי מחייב בעל הכלב או לא וכמו שדרכו ודרך הגאונים לפסוק ככל את"ל

ה) שם במימרא דרבא
פי' שנשך הכלב את המשסה

bet) Straightforward from Bava Kamma 24b. Rashi explains that it is indirect causation in damages. The Beit Yosef writes that according to the Rambam he nevertheless remains liable under the laws of Heaven, as explained above in simanim 378 and 386.

gimel) In my humble opinion the Rambam learned this from Rava's statement there introduced by 'if you say,' regarding one who incites another's dog against a person. This implies that the question whether the dog's owner is liable was resolved, following the Rambam's and the Geonim's general practice of ruling according to an 'if you say' formulation.

dalet) The Maggid Mishneh writes that even if the dog was forewarned, since it did not act on its own but only because it was incited, it is like an arena ox, concerning which the verse teaches 'if it gores,' but not if others cause it to gore; such an ox is exempt from death. Here too its status is that of a tam.
heh) Ibid., in Rava's statement. The meaning is that the dog bit the person who incited it.

he_segments: ג) שם ס"ב ושם בגמ' מכריז רב יוסי ואתימא רבה וכו'
ד) כן כתב רש"י והרא"ש שם

dalet) Rashi and the Rosh likewise write there.

heh) The language of the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 5, and so writes the Rif, and so appears in the Gemara. However, insofar as the Rambam writes there that the same law applies to all animals, we do not rule like him. Rashi explains that the ruling applies even on a day that is not a market day.

bet) Ibid., in the Gemara, 'sold for plowing.' The Maggid Mishneh explains that the purchaser may initially plow with it, and that the sale remains valid and neither party may retract. He appears to understand the baraita according to Rabbi Akiva, who says there that the injured party and owner are partners, and derives this from the law that if the owner consecrated the ox the consecration takes effect because of Rabbi Abbahu's principle. According to Rabbi Yishmael, who treats the injured party as a creditor, Rabbi Abbahu's rule would not be needed.
gimel) Ibid., in the Gemara. The meaning is that in our time, when beit din does not collect the penalty, if the injured party seized the ox it is not removed from him.
dalet) Explained in the sugya there according to Rabbi Akiva, whose view is followed against an individual colleague.

he_segments: ק) שם ס"ח וברמב"ם שם די"ב וכתב ה"ה הוא כשמואל דבגמרא ולא כרב והטעם מפני שכל אלו הנזקין תולדות בור ולא מצינו בור שחייב בו את הכלים

a) The baraita there. Rashi explains that the pipe carries household wastewater into the public domain.

ז) שם במשנה
en_segments: a) The language of the Rambam, chapter 13 of Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon, law 14, from the Mishnah in the third chapter of Bava Kamma 30a and Rav Ashi's interpretation there. The meaning is that the material is placed there to fertilize fields and vineyards.
bet) Ibid., in the Mishnah, following Rav that liability concerns both the substance itself and its increase in value, on 30b.
gimel) Straightforward from the Gemara there according to Rav Nachman's answer.

dalet) The Rosh writes this in his rulings from the Gemara's interpretation. The Beit Yosef and Kesef Mishneh write that the Rambam views that interpretation as a mere rejection. In my humble opinion, although there is an explicit statement of Rav Huna in the name of Rav there, the Rambam understood that Rav retracted it in the sugya at the beginning of 51a.
heh) The Gemara's interpretation there.

vav) An unresolved question there. Following his general approach in uncertainties of monetary law, the Rambam holds that if the claimant seized, it is not removed from him. The Tur writes likewise in the name of the Ramah.
zayin) Ibid., in the Mishnah.

he_segments: י) שם דין י"ג כ' ה"ה בעיא דרבא שם ואמר את"ל כיון דלא אמדוהו יהיב ליה דמי כולו וכו' ופסק כאת"ל וכן דרך רבינו בגמרא:
כ) כן היא שם בגמ' ברמב"ם ובטור
פירו' כאלו עשה הכל בפע' אחת שאינו עולה כ"כ כמו שאומדין כל אחת בפני עצמו תוס'
ל) וכן כ' ה"ה שם בשם התו' ושלזה הסכים הרשב"א ואפשר שזה דעת רבינו הרמב"ם ז"ל
מ) שם ושם בגמרא בעיא דלא איפשטא
נ) כ' ה"ה פי' אחר שנגרעו דמיו מחסרון ידו ורגלו דודאי אם תפס דמי כולו כמו שהיה בריא מפקינן מיניה וא"ת הכל עולה לחשבון א' לא היה דחילוק יש בין שומ' אחת לשומות הרבה כדאמרינן לעיל
en_segments: yud) Ibid., law 13. The Maggid Mishneh writes that this is Rava's question there, followed by an 'if you say': since they did not first assess him, he gives him the value of the entire injury. The Rambam rules according to the 'if you say,' as is his general practice in the Gemara.

kaf) So appears in the Gemara, Rambam, and Tur. The meaning is that the injuries are treated as though they were all inflicted at one time, because the total appraisal is then less than the sum of separate appraisals, Tosafot.
lamed) The Maggid Mishneh writes likewise there in the name of Tosafot, and that the Rashba agreed. It is possible that this is also the Rambam's view.
mem) Ibid., an unresolved question in the Gemara.

nun) The Maggid Mishneh explains that this refers to the value after his worth was already reduced by the loss of his hand and foot. Certainly, if the injured party seized the full value he had when healthy, it is removed from him. If all the appraisals necessarily produced the same total, there would be no issue, but there is a difference between one combined appraisal and multiple appraisals, as stated above.

he_segments: ה) טור סי"ט משנה בפ"ג דל"ג ע"א
ו) שם בשם אביו הרא"ש שם בפסקיו

ז) וכ' מהר"ם מרוזבורג ☜ראובן טען על שמעון שקראו ממזר ושמעון אומר שמתחל' לחש לו באזנו שהוא ממזר לכן נתרגז וא"ל כן אומדנא דמוכח הוי כיון שקראו פתאום ממזר ודאי האמת אתו עכ"ל וא"צ לישבע ע"ז כמ"ש לעיל סימן ת"כ סל"ח סמ"ע בשם ד"מ
ח) וכ' בנימוקי מהר"ם דדין אשה לענין בזיון כדין איש ואם אין האיש רוצ' שתתבזה אשתו צריך לפדותה בממון כפי אשר ישיתו עליו הב"ד וע' לעיל סי' תכד ס"ח מזה סמ"ע בשם ד"מ
ט) שם ושם:
י) שם ושם:
כ) כ' המרדכי פרק המניח אין לדחוף אדם את חבירו כשמכין זה את זה אלא יש לשומטו בנחת ואם דחף חייב לעשות לו דין ונלע"ד שלמדו מדין שור שעלה ע"ג שור מבואר בסי' שפ"ג ס"ב
en_segments: heh) Tur, seif 19, from the Mishnah in the third chapter on 33a.
vav) Ibid., in the name of his father the Rosh in his rulings. The meaning is after the parties had separated from one another. See above in siman 420.

zayin) Maharam of Rothenburg writes: Reuven claimed that Shimon called him a mamzer. Shimon responded that Reuven had first whispered in his ear that Shimon was a mamzer, and therefore Shimon became enraged and called him that. This is a compelling circumstantial inference, because if Shimon suddenly called him a mamzer, it is evident that his account is true. He therefore need not swear concerning this, as written above in siman 420, seif 38, Sema in the name of Darkei Moshe.

chet) Nimukei Maharam writes that a woman's status regarding humiliation is the same as a man's. If a husband does not wish his wife to be humiliated, he must redeem her through monetary payment in the amount assessed by beit din. See above in siman 424, seif 8, Sema in the name of Darkei Moshe.
tet) Ibid., in the same source.
yud) Ibid., in the same source.

kaf) The Mordechai in chapter HaMeniach writes that when two people are fighting, one should not shove the other, but should disengage gently. If he shoves him, he is liable for the resulting injury. In my humble opinion, this was learned from the law of an ox that mounted another ox, explained in siman 383, seif 2.

he_segments: פ) ל' הרמב"ם שם פרק ד' דין י' מברייתא פ"ב דע"א דף כ"ו ע"ב וסוגיא דגמרא שם ויש נוסחא אחרת בב"י והעתיק' בי"ד סי' קנ"ח סי"א וע"ש
צ) הן הוא ברמב"ם שם וכ' הכ"מ בפלוגתא דרב אחא ורבינא וכו' שם פסק כמ"ד מותר להכעיס אפיקורס הוא ועוד דר' אבהו ור' יוחנן סברי הכי שם:

tzadi) So appears in the Rambam there. The Kesef Mishneh writes that in the dispute of Rav Acha and Ravina the Rambam rules according to the view that one who sins in order to provoke is an apikores. Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yochanan likewise hold this view there.
kuf) Ibid., in the baraita, as the Amoraim explain it there.
reish) This means that the statement taught at the end of Kiddushin, 'the best among the gentiles, kill,' refers to a time of war, as Tosafot write in the name of the Yerushalmi.

shin) Chazal said this only regarding the gentiles of their time, who worshipped stars and constellations and did not believe in the Exodus from Egypt or creation of the world. But the nations under whose protection the Jewish people presently live and among whom we are dispersed believe in creation, the Exodus from Egypt, and the fundamentals of religion, and direct their intent toward the Creator of heaven and earth, as the poskim write and the Rama cites in Orach Chaim siman 126 in a gloss. Not only is it not prohibited to save them, we are even obligated to pray for their welfare. The author of Maaseh Hashem explains this at length in his commentary on the Haggadah to the verse, 'Pour out Your wrath upon the nations that do not know You': King David prayed against those nations that do not believe in creation or in the signs and wonders Hashem performed for us in Egypt and at Matan Torah. The nations under whose protection we live believe in all these matters, as stated, and we remain steadfast in continually praying for the welfare of the government and its ministers, for their success, and for all the lands under their rule. The Rambam writes that the halakhah follows Rabbi Yehoshua in Sanhedrin 105a, chapter Chelek, that even the righteous among the nations have a share in the World to Come.

tav) The Kesef Mishneh explains that the phrase means one who does not persist continually in wickedness, excluding a shepherd of small livestock. Although such shepherds act for their own benefit out of greed for money, they remain constantly engaged in wrongdoing. It also excludes one who eats neveilot deliberately to provoke, for even if he does not constantly persist in that wrongdoing, he is included among the apikorsim, as explained at the beginning of the seif.
